query: I'm considering upgrading my ebike controller to a more powerful option and I'm curious about the benefits of moving from a 48v 22ah to a 48v 30ah controller. Is it really worth the investment, and how much of a difference in speed and performance can I expect? Also, how does the upgrade process work if I want to get the 48v 30ah controller since it's not listed on Amazon? Any insights would be appreciated!
ori_review:
So, this was kinda expensive, but well worth the investment.
Upgraded my Super73 Z1 from its original controller 36v 11ah
Purchased this set 48v 22ah as upgrade. Purchased 48v 20ah battery to match controller voltage, too.

Controller and display are great but….I ended up burning out a MOSFET.
I contacted company for replacement since I was still under warranty.

Company did not have a 48v 22ah in stock at time so they offered to UPGRADE my replacement with a 48v 30ah controller. Only had to pay $20 shipping.

I don’t think I will ever go back to anything less than 48v 30ah for a controller. I thought 48v 22ah was powerful.
The speed and takeoff are even more amazing with 48v 30ah controller.

You can see the difference in size of controller with just a few more amp hours added. But boy what a difference!
(Pic bottom image 22ah controller; top image 30ah controller)

They don’t sell the 48v 30ah controller on Amazon, but if you email them when u make your purchase, you can upgrade. And I strongly urge you to.
48v 30ah has to be experienced to believe!!

Matter of fact, 48v 30ah controller is so much better than 48v 22 ah that comes with order (which definitely ain’t bad) that I ordered a second set and paid full price for upgraded controller and display ($139 + $20 upgrade fee) to have when I build/mod my next ebike.

Well worth the money, imo. Hope this review helps.

ori_review:
Love it! It's nice heavy fabric and seems to be strongly stitched. I own an Umarex Legends full-auto MP40 airgun (which is AWESOME!) and there are two things specific to the Umarex MP40 you should know about if you're buying this for it.

First, the bolt handle doesn't go all the way forward, which was the Lock position on the original. The reinforcement patch on the side thus doesn't quite cover the bolt handle. Won't be an issue for me, it's always treated nicely. Second, the Legends BB magazine is 1/2" inch longer than the 9mm original. The lower three mag pouches fit the mags fine and look good. The top two mag pouches won't close over the Legends magazine, too short. You could punch a new hole in the strap, but the flap would ride up too far and look weird. No problem unless you have four or more magazines.

IT'S PERFECT ANYWAY! I stash my two magazines in the lower pouches, and one holds a tube of BBs. The top two slots store my CO2 carts (6-8 each). The square pouch holds my C02 wrench and the loading-assist tool I made. The gun is stored protected with all ammo, gas, and tools needed for a long session of machine pistol goodness. It also looks like I stole it from a Wehrmacht officer's luggage, a level of realism needed for such a nice replica gun.

If you have a genuine MP40 (lucky bastard) it will probably fit perfectly. It works fine for the Legends replica with the caveats above.

query: I'm 6'4" and I'm looking for a double sleeping bag that fits comfortably for both me and my wife. Can you provide tips on how to properly stuff it back into the sack, since I find it challenging to pack it away? Any advice on the best folding technique would be appreciated!

It does not roll up and slide in, that is not what a stuff sack is.  You grab the bottom of the bag fold in half, then half again.  So now its in quarters at the bottom.  Stuff the bottom into the stuff sack, and then just keep shoving more and more of the bag into the sack.  When you have it all shoved in, cinch the top closed, adjust the compression straps in a crisscross on the top, and pull on the compression straps on the side of the stuff sack.

query: What are some tips for assembling the darts for my blowgun, and how can I improve my shooting technique for better accuracy? I’ve found the assembly process to be a bit challenging, and I want to ensure I'm using it effectively to hit my targets consistently.
ori_review:
I love this blowgun. For what it is, it's capable of surprising accuracy. My only complaint is that it was unnecessarily hard to assemble the darts. The trick is as follows:

1) Grasp the shaft of a dart about an inch from the sharp end with a pair of pliers.

2) Allow the cup to sit upright on a piece of scrap wood, and slowly press the sharp end of the dart all the way through the cup to the other side. Try to go in as straight as you can.

3) Pull the cup free, reverse the shaft so your pliers are now an inch or so from the dull end, and force the dull end into the hole you just made until you are just short of coming through the other side. It won't come apart now under normal use, don't be too worried if it's not perfectly straight, it matters less than you probably think.

My current shooting technique is to hold the mid shaft of the blowgun with my right hand, and the mouthpiece with my left. When I stand square to the target and focus on it, I see two images of the front sight. The dart will strike exactly in the middle of those two images. (I've noticed that if I reverse my hand positions, the dart will not longer strike in the middle - I suspect it has to do with eye dominance but I really have no idea).

The first trick is to not move the shaft after blowing the air in. The second trick is to continue to provide breath until the dart exits the muzzle. The third trick is to deliver the same amount of air for each shot. It's fun, but it's not easy. It feels kind of like archery.

A cardboard box is all the target you need. My best five-shot group so far was about the size of a fifty cent piece, from 20 feet away. I think it's capable of even more than that.

query: I'm curious about the battery life of these heated socks. How long can I expect them to last on a single charge, especially when using the highest setting? Also, how warm does it actually feel when using the maximum temperature? I’m looking for socks that provide warmth for outdoor activities like skiing or hiking, and I want to ensure they perform well in cold conditions.
ori_review: [[VIDEOID:974b9a81d630248e6d3fd6478c15aa2b]] I found these socks to be nicely made with good quality material and stitching. The heating element is mainly under the toes and forward ball of the foot with the wires running alongside the foot and ankle to avoid pressure points. The heating pads are thin and you can definitely feel them when you walk but it's the kind of presence that you can get used to after a while. The top cuff has a deep pocket on the side in which to stuff the battery and wire. It bulges out a bit but is not a problem to cover with your pant leg. How long do the batteries last on one charge? It's not stated in the product description but it is in the owner's manual that came with the socks. Setting 1 (highest, 55°C) lasts 4-5 hours; setting 2 (45°C) lasts 6-7 hours; setting 3 (38°C) lasts 9-10 hours. I tested it on the max setting (#1) and got around 5 hours of warmth during mixed usage indoors and outdoors (35°F, 2°C). This was consistent with the claimed duration in the owners manual. How hot does it feel? 55°C (131°F) merely feels warm but that is how these heated foot devices work. I've used heated insoles in ski boots for decades and they work by taking the edge off the cold though gentle warmth. These socks work the same way. I have not run an extended test on these yet so I won't comment on how they hold up through many wash cycles and many charge cycles; I'll update later as appropriate. But my initial reaction to these socks is very positive. They are made well and work as designed. Nice!

I started buying motorcycle helmets in the early 70s and have never had trouble. Had a Brancale in the mid-80's (what a joke those were). Bicycle helmets have always been problematic to get a good one which fits properly and therefore is safe. If one must use that clicker on the headband for than one or 2 clicks then, I believe that one is sacrificing comfort and safety. I have found that if one is frugal and takes ones time a lot of money does not need to be spent in order to procure a good looking safe helmet. I speak from experience as I have lost track of how many helmets I have destroyed: a few motorcycle helmets, a hang glider helmet, and a few bicycle helmets.

Most anglers straight retrieve this plug, but I catch a lot of fish on this bait by jerking it around and retrieving it at different speeds with some twitches and pauses in between, sometimes just on a simple straight retrieve  but it seems to work better with a little bit more erratic of an action, almost like how you would work a smaller jerkbait for largemouth but Striper love that presentation. What actually prompted me to come on here and write this review about just how effective this plug is, is the fact that the second fish I caught today was while I was doing absolutely nothing while the bait was legit just floating there in the water. I got hit by a wave and got way more wet than I expected and stopped for about five seconds to just get my footing and lone and behold a striper literally hit it while it was just sitting there. The lure casts incredibly far which is why I believe it is one of the most effective surfcasting plugs for striper, it’s pretty much the ideal one size fits all type profile, as it’s not TOO big to completely alienate smaller schoolies, but it is a large enough profile to primarily target the bigger fish. I mean this thing will go half a mile even on lighter tackle. If you don’t have at least one or two of these things in your tacklebox what are you even doing??

query: I'm looking for a blowup mattress that is easy to set up and stow away. I also want to know how it compares to regular blowup mattresses. Can you recommend a product that meets these criteria, especially for camping or hosting guests?
ori_review:
If you're looking for a sign, this is the one! This is the most incredible blowup mattress I have every owned. Setting it up and stowing it away is truly a breeze. Once I laid it out flat I was able to pump it up with my foot is less and 60 seconds. The first night we took this for a spin we joined another couple who brought a tall, queen size blowup mattress. But what is the difference in this product and a regular blowup mattress? The design! The "drawstring" design to be exact. Blowup mattresses are notorious for being completely flat, so when pressure is applied to one side, it makes the opposite side swell as the air distributes to that end. Because this mattress is a bunch of mini-cushions separated by these little ripples, it allows air to be distributed evenly around where pressure is applied. This prevents any other part of the mattress from bulging. This designs makes sleeping next to someone less annoying bc you aren't feeling every single movement the other person makes. We think this is such a great mattress that we will use it in the event we have company but not enough spots to sleep. Put this on the floor and pair it with a pillow and a blanket and this thing is better than 30% of bed mattresses on the market today.

We paired this with Amazon's sleeping bag, "MEREZA Double Sleeping Bag for Adults" and experienced luxury camping for an exceptionally affordable price. As an avid reviewer, this product receives my highest recommend, and is in the top 5 best products I purchased from Amazon in 2022.

query: I'm looking for a saddle that can provide comfort for riders with wider sit bones, as my current saddle is causing pain and numbness. ori_review:
This might not be lightest or slickest saddle money can buy, but who cares. I was initially attracted to this saddle because it is one of the few saddles available that seems to keep riders with wider sit bones comfortable. I bought this saddle to replace the Specialized 'Body Geometry' saddle that came that came with my new Rockhopper, that was causing me to have pain and some numbness. This saddle instantly eliminated all of the pain and numbness that came as a result of the old saddles rounded top profile that was putting pressure between my sit bones. The Purve V has a very flat profile that hence its name has a consistent V taper from front to back. This allows the Pure V, with proper adjustment, to hit the sit bones correctly for a much broader range of riders than the rounded racing style saddles that are meant to hinder the legs less. Yet, chaffing and leg pressure has not been an issue for me on 60+ mile rides.

As a bonus the Pure V is padded with a firm and supportive material that is neither too thick nor thin, that provides just the right amount of padding to make this saddle very comfortable to ride long distances even without a chamois. This is the only saddle Ive ridden to date that has made effective use of the "love channel" that alleviates pressure between the sit bones that might be caused by the slight cushiness of this saddle. I would definitely recommend this saddle to anyone looking for a solid versatile and comfortable saddle.

query: I'm looking for a pedal exerciser that can fit under my desk, ideally something easy to assemble and heavy enough to stay in place while I use it. I need it to have adjustable tension settings for a comfortable workout while I'm working on my computer, and it would be great if it has a digital display to track my progress. Also, I'm concerned about the design—does it slide around easily, and how do I manage the battery life for the digital display? Any tips or advice would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Assembly of this unit was simple. There is a wrench tool included to tighten the bolts. This unit is kind of heavy, which is great because if it were too light, it would slide around too easily. I spend so much time in front of the computer that it had affected my health because I wasn't getting any exercise in. With this device, there is no excuse. It fits perfectly under my desk (make sure to compare dimensions of the height of this item to your desk). I have a clearance of 23 1/2" and it has been just enough height for me to use this comfortably. I have roller chairs so purchasing something like [[ASIN:B000X8X58S Slipstick CB840 3-1/4 Inch Bed Roller / Furniture Wheel Gripper Caster Cups (Set of 4) Caramel Color]] was essential for securing my chair in place while using this exercise bike under my table without my chair rolling all over the place.

The different tension resistances are nice and click into place easily. Even at the highest setting, the resistance does not seem too bad and I can easily cycle if I'm pedaling slowly. If I pedal quickly at the highest tension setting, I'll start to build up a sweat after not too long, but if you're in the workplace using this, you probably don't want to go all out and smell like you just got out of the gym around your co-workers. At home alone, I can get in my workout in the morning while working on the computer and then just shower before heading to work. It's perfect for my needs. The non-slip feet seem to hold it securely in place on my chairmat with the edge of the unit against the wall. If I did not have it against the wall, it might slide around a little more than I'd probably like. A simple solution would be to place some strong double-sided tape along the bottom of the rubber feet. The digital display is powered by 2 AAA batteries and it is attached to the cycle so it is not removable. Also, there doesn't seem to be an on/off switch to the LED display so you'll have to remove your batteries when it's not in use to save on your battery life. However, if you leave the batteries in, it'll turn off by itself after about 5 minutes of inactivity. Likewise, if you leave the batteries in and the unit is off, the digital reader will turn on by itself and start measuring your activity if you start cycling. If I'm just cycling and don't care about the stats, I just leave the digital display alone with the batteries out. The foot straps securely hold your feet in place. Overall, the many benefits of this outweigh the minor design drawbacks. This is easily one of the best investments I've made.

Pros
-Adjustable tension easily clicks into place
-Digital device measures progress
-Easy assembly
-Footstraps hold feet in securely
-Quiet

Cons
-Must remove batteries to turn off digital device
-May slide around if not secured with tape or backed against wall

query: I'm looking for a baitcasting reel that can handle heavier setups for fishing in the Florida intracoastal and also serve as a lighter option for surf fishing. Are there any models similar to the Millionaire Classic that would meet these needs? Also, how do I handle the spool release to avoid straining the anti-reverse mechanism? Any recommendations would be appreciated!
ori_review:
This is the tried and true Millionaire Classic with new colors and carbon fiber drag.

I bought this to fish as a heavier setup for the Florida intracoastal and light setup for the surf. My main surf reels are Daiwa Sealine x30sha but I wanted something lighter to put on a 9' rod to fish the first trough. I have only caught a few winter bluefish between 11" and 18" so far but the reel handled them easily.

The new color scheme is black and it looks great on the all metal body and the gold spool tensioner. Everything is smooth and the drag adjustment turns nicely.

I can cast 73 yards on a 9' rod, 4 oz sinker, stock greased bearings, and with the line leveler in place. It feels very fast though, and if you cleaned the bearings and removed the line leveler I think you could easily cast over 100. I have my Sealines for long casting though so I'm leaving this as is.

The size is comparable to an Abu Garcia 6000 series. You can see the comparison to my larger reels in the pictures.

The only issue - and this is for all reels with a bar and/or button release (as opposed to clutch switch) - is that you need to use your thumb to roll the spool back a little before you put it into free spool if you are using heavy rigs. Otherwise, it feels to me like you are putting extra strain on the anti reverse.

I did open it up to add extra grease to the main gears but they were already well greased. Looked clean inside.

I've had it to the beach a few times, and with a fresh water rinse afterwards, it seems to be holding up just fine.

Highly recommend.

query: I'm looking for a pannier set that is suitable for commuting rather than touring. just to help other people without them having to check the web for the volumes of the various axiom panniers, since i looked them all up i figured i would save you all the trouble:

pannier volumes:
Seymour LX [this set]
1700c" (27.85L) per pair
Seymour DLX 30
1830c" (30L) per pair
Lasalle DLX 45
1830c" (30L) per pair
Cartier DLX 35
2013c" (33L) per pair
Kootenay DLX
2441c" (40L) per pair
Champlain DLX 60
3000c" (49L) per pair

that said, i also own this set and love em. they mount pretty decently to my rear axiom rack as well as my front jim blackburn rack. you have to pull pretty firmly to release the clips, which is good because my last set of panniers kept leaping off.

so far the bottom bungee is holding well. its thinner than the other pannier models bungees, but with repeated removal the bungee like any of them will stretch so you will have to eventually replace it.

the bungee on this model is the same size as the one on the appalachian set, it took a good 3 years of constant removal for those to lose all of their elasticity though but they still hold, they just no longer stretch.

like any non-rubber pannier set these are water RESIS|TANT but by no means water-proof. if you intend on using them in downpours, plan accordingly and either use dry sacks on the inside or buy or make exteriour rain covers.

waterproofing sprays will eventually wear off, which is just a "feature" of waterproofing sprays.

this model is more for a commute than for touring. they have a rear pouch for easy access to first aid, tools, etc and i think its an improvement over the appalachian side mounted pouches which really just make them stick out more. the pouches are also low which is going to keep your weight where it belongs.

like most single clip on panniers these sit about an inch and a half above the rear racks flat area, so while a rear trunk will fit nicely in the middle of the bags, a basket or crate will not.

unlike the appalachian panniers, these are separate pieces that you can either use as just one to suit your needs or together. they also snap together at the handles for carrying when not on the rack.

the only thing i would like to see on these bags is make exteriour webbing like they have on the other models and included rain covers

query: I'm looking for a hitch-mounted bike rack that can accommodate various bike sizes without needing constant adjustments. I want something that allows for quick loading and unloading and has a secure locking mechanism. I've considered options like the Thule 917XT, Yakima Holdup, and Saris Cycle On Pro, but I need to ensure it fits my needs for transporting different types of bikes, including mountain and children's bikes. Can you help me find a rack that meets these criteria?
ori_review:
I purchased this rack on Amazon and got the best deal out there for $340 and free shipping. I would have gone with the 916XT, but unfortunately, my car only had a capacity for a class II hitch, so 917XT it was!

I lamented for days over the Thule 917XT, Yakima Holdup and Saris Cycle On Pro. All of the racks have disadvantages and advantages depending on your application. I chose the Thule for a bunch of reasons, but the one which made the biggest difference was being able to load/unload different style bikes in seconds(Mountain, Beach, BMX, Larger Children's bikes) without having to adjust the front wheel mount. The Yakima seemed to be a one size fits all with the flip down tire mount which didn't seem to be what I needed for my application given it would be me and one of my kids bikes which range in all different sizes. I liked the Yakima's compact size when folded up, but I also had concerns should the mount wiggle loose and having it damage my car. The Saris Cycle On has an excellent price point and great hitch lock/tightening feature that I really liked, BUT, if I was carrying anything less than a 26in bike, I had to adjust the front wheel mount by unscrewing bolts and moving the mount to the smaller adjustment to accomodate the smaller tire up to a 20in. This was too much work for what I needed and I would have potentially been changing this every other day.

All three racks have a no touch frame grab bar, that only makes contact with the front tire. This is invalueable if you cherish your bikes finish OR have an expensive bike where you could potentially damage the top tube when using similar racks like the Yakima Stickup or Thule Doubletrack which are about $100 cheaper. I also liked the fact that I could adjust the angle and position of the tire grab bar. The Yakima is identical to the Thule and the Saris is fixed position. I liked that all of the racks had a security locking device and the 917XT came WITH the hitch STL2 hitchlock and locking cylinders for the grab bars. Remember that these are only deterrents and a determined thief can get it if they want it bad enough. A lot of reviewers dinged the rack in the security aspect which I don't believe is fair. If its that important, take extra measures by buying additonal cable locks if you intend on leaving your bikes on the rack unattended for an extended period of time.

The Thule rack is fantastic all around. I load my bike(s) quickly and they don't move. It only takes seconds to load and you are off. The rack tilts up when not in use and will tilt down to access the trunk/liftgate with the bikes still loaded on the rack. It was well worth the money. I did have a beef with how it the package was treated when being shipped as the box was crushed and the end split open. One of the cross bars was chipped, but it wasn't worth sending it back as I would have incurred shipping charges to return it for such a small blemish. Nevertheless, I give this rack 5 stars for its ease of operation and features that fit what I needed. You can go to Youtube and look at a side by side comparison which was VERY helpful for me...looking at a picture is one thing, but watching the pros who sell these things all day long do a demo is priceless in seeing what you are getting.

If not for my different bike size dilemma, I would have purchase the Saris Cycle On Pro as a side note. It had what I was looking for and was $100 cheaper with free shipping on Amazon ($247), I just couldn't justify constantly changing the mount by unbolting it.

query: I'm looking for a lightweight backpack that can comfortably hold about 12lbs of gear. I want to know if this pack has features that allow for good organization, like pockets for a water filter and a toilet kit, while also being durable and waterproof. ori_review: My base weight is around 12lbs. or a little less and this pack can't be beaten for that size of a load. I've worn it for a grand total of about 12 miles so far, just trying to dial in the fit and the comfort level, so I won't be able to speak to long-term durability yet, but I'm confident I can provide a solid overview of this pack. Inside the pack, even though the fabric is waterproof, the seams aren't taped so I line it with a trash compactor bag. A sleeping bag, clothes bag, sleeping pad, and puffy jacket fit nicely squeezed into the bottom. I usually carry an Ursack inside a waterproof sea to summit ultrasil bag that includes my food and cook kit just above the other stuff in the middle of the pack. For now, the tent is in the pack next to the food bag, but I imagine I'll have to carry it on the outside after a wet night. What you see in the first picture is the bag packed with all of those items and it fits extremely well. The outside zippered pocket includes my toilet kit and my tent stakes. Behind that front pocket is my ditty bag and a polycryo groundsheet for my tent, as can be seen in the picture. One of the side pockets is a little taller than the others, which is probably where I will keep a wet tent, but both side pockets easily hold 1-liter smart water bottles as shown. You can't see it, but my Katadyn BeFree water filter is in the side pocket with one of the water bottles. The Z-seat nicely sits on the top under the strap and my trowel is on a carabiner hanging off a daisy chain on one side. Arranged this way, the pack is as comfortable as any I've ever worn, including my GG Crown2. I've not fully loaded it down with water but I can't imagine those last few pounds would make much of a difference. The only problem I've run into has been the hipbelt slipping down a bit after a couple of miles, where I have to make an adjustment or cinch or pretty tight to keep it from sliding. I'll update the review once I've gotten a hundred or miles on it and revisit the durability but at the moment it seems like one hell of a tough pack. Oh, and one last thing about the hip belt pockets. They are just barely big enough to fit my iPhone XR, but the zippers are sort of closer to the middle of the pouch than the top. These are perfect for improving your balance. I also noticed after walking for about ten minutes in them that my heart rate was up, I was sweating, and I could feel my inner and outer thigh muscles, glutes, hip flexor muscles and core(Stomach) muscles being engaged and worked. These Kangoo Jumps, force you to stand up straight so that's good for your posture too. You can bounce in them and run in them. I haven't been able to jump up and down in them yet with both feet because the springs are still tight. But I can bounce one leg at a time and run in them without knee pain. But carrying these jumps for more than a five blocks or so is not IDEAL they are heavy. Over all I'm enjoying them, and I get stopped on the streets constantly by tourist who're curious about them. query: I'm looking for a small, adjustable focus LED flashlight that uses AAA batteries. I want something bright but don't necessarily need multiple brightness settings. I've seen some flashlights that have zoom features, but I’m curious if this one also allows for easy zooming. I’ve read mixed things about the brightness levels and whether they truly change, so I’d like to know more about its performance and if it’s reliable for regular use.
ori_review:
I've got about a dozen LED flashlights - most bought that way and some are retrofits (a Maglite, a Rayovac, and a 1st gen SnakeLight). They vary in brightness from 30 or so lumens up to 800 lumens. My favorite is my EDC (every day carry) Mini MLR2 that's 1/2 inch shorter than my chapstick and has 7 settings, including a high setting of 180 lumens. I'm currently jonesin' for a $120 L3 K40 with 1147 lumens and 700 meter beam distance - that thing is FRIGGIN' AWESOME! Now, I'm no flashaholic . . . ok - scratch that. I guess my point is that even though I didn't need this little adjustable focus, 3 aaa, cree led flashlight, and it doesn't do everything the description says it would do, and it has middle of the road brightness (compared to other led lights), I STILL love it. Just like a $3 bottle of Oak Leaf Pinot Grigio from Walmart, for $9.90 this flashlight was nearly guaranteed to please. Admittedly, as long as it didn't short-circuit and cook my fingers like grilled kielbasa, I was probably going to like it. Using only 3 aaa batteries, this thing throws a beam that will make you wonder why you'd want any flashlight that's more powerful (trust me - you will). It will also zoom out and cast a flood that's very impressive. What it DOESN'T do is strobe or change brightness, even though the description says it will. You know what? I'm giving it 5 stars anyway. I do recommend taking it apart and using some di-electric grease (silicone lubricant) on the rubber o-ring where the head slides to zoom in and out. Doing this will make it easier to work the zoom. Go ahead and put some on the threads, too. Bottom line? If you haven't seen what they're doing with flashlights these days, you will absolutely be amazed by this purchase. In fact, for less than ten bucks, you too can begin a life of searching for more lumens/$ and trying to justify/rationalize your every flashlight purchase to yourself, your friends, and your therapist. Do yourself a favor and buy it, then give your old incandescent flashlights to Goodwill, the Salvation Army, your so-called friends, or your judgmental therapist. Now - I'm off to look at the K40 website. Again.

Edit: I see the description has been changed and no longer says it changes brightness or strobes. This flashlight gets used regularly and is still a 5 star purchase.

Edit to my previous Edit: They're claiming again that this light has three brightness level choices. It does not. There is a single brightness with no change in battery consumption. I love the zoom feature, but changing the zoom function does not equate to changing brightness. To clarify, the zoom is a continuous slide from spot to flood - there is no setting for spot, flood, or area (and what the heck is the difference between area and flood, anyway?!?). This thing still gets 5 stars from me, but I wish they'd get a better translator.

Update: Just received my third one. I bought it as a gift for someone who will be hiking in Peru. This, along with an [[ASIN:B00C1KI8Q0 Olight I3S 80 Lumen Cree XP-G2 LED LED Flashlight (Black Body) with 3 X EdisonBright AAA batteries]] (also uses an AAA battery and can clip to the brim of a hat), should provide versatile lighting that only uses one type of easily obtained battery. I'm ordering 2 more for some nephews who are in Scouting. Since theirs might get used infrequently, I'm also ordering [[ASIN:B00AHKUOPY Energizer Advanced Lithium AAA Batteries 6 Pack - EA92BP4F2]] ($8.74 shipped) to guarantee against leakage. In fact, I'd recommend that battery or Eneloops rather than alkalines, especially if the light sees infrequent use.

query: I'm looking for an electric bike that is suitable for taller riders, ideally one that offers good range and speed. I want something that rides well and has a solid build, as I'm about 6'2" tall and prefer a bike that can handle my height comfortably.
ori_review:
This is the best ebike I’ve ever own and between my wife and I we’ve own 7 so far. It ride fantastic however, I replace the pogo stick they call a “suspension seat post”. Fair warning this is a BIG bike for taller people. I’m 6’2” tall and it’s great. The frame is very long and heavy. I have ridden 34+ miles on a single charge and I’m guessing it could have gone to 50 miles. I was riding in peddle assist at lower speeds (about 12/hour).

Big negative is the stupid way they program the peddle assist. If you set it for true peddle assist the motor will only run while you are peddling. While the throttle does work it is limited to the assist number you are in at the time. So if you need to make a quick acceleration forget it. You can also set it to throttle assist which is simply a modification of the other peddle assist except the throttle is alway live a available. The draw back is it too is limited to what ever assist level is chosen. So if you power up the bike you must choose a power level. If you want full power available to you you need to press the up arrow 5 times. Then the throttle will work normally. Very strange.

If you need service you are basically calling some guy that I think is actually in China. Not to say this is bad but his response to my problem was to take it to a local bike shop and they could fix my problem. Duh! Option 2 was a Parks Tool Company video that he sent me a link to. While this may not sound like great service I can tell you it’s a lot better then the service I got from the people I bought my wife’s new ebike from.

Bottom line …. if your a taller person this is a very nice bike with good range and speed (25 to 28 MPH on a full pack). I’ve had it for about a month and just got my first 100 miles on it. Would have more but I split my riding time with 2 other bike still. But because of how well it handles and rides I’m now thinking of selling my other bikes.

query: I'm looking for a bike trainer that provides a workout similar to outdoor riding. I've set it up in my unheated garage and want to know how to best install it, especially regarding the rear axle since my quick-release handle can be tricky. Also, I would appreciate better instructions or an assembly video for guidance. I've noticed that the tensioner doesn't seem effective, and I prefer adjusting difficulty through my bike's gears. Overall, I'm curious about the durability of this trainer after a good initial experience. Can anyone share their thoughts or experiences related to these concerns?
ori_review:
Before I write the cons and pros, here's some context: 70 year old, typically ride 45-75 minutes each day around flat streets of neighborhood when weather permits; median speed: 12 +/- 1 mph. Weather here now has too much ice and snow on roads, so I purchased this trainer. Our house is small, so I set up the trainer in our unheated garage.

Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF): while I have no idea of the durability of the product, it provided a terrific workout that simulated a real bike ride far better than I expected. The "pros" described below far outweighed the 'cons".

Cons (starting with the bad stuff first):
1. Changing rear axle: I hated having to change axles; it was necessary because my quick release handle won't allow the stand to latch. When I was pulling the regular axle out and installing theirs, the wheel and chain slipped, so I had to figure out how to get the chain back on properly. Now I'm hoping that I can just leave this axle on when I return to riding outdoors {manufacturer: that's a question to you].
2. Instructions: Instructions are really not good, just as other reviews have said. It took me quite a while to figure out how to position the roller such that I could mount the bike's axle onto their latching system. Then I had to guess how much to tighten the roller screw. The manufacturer should provide an assembly video that is roughly twice as long and shows each step being performed completely.
3. Tensioner: it's basically worthless. There was no difference between 0-8. I'm probably just going to take it off the handlebars and set it on the ground behind the bike stand.

Pros:
1. Great workout: I was surprised at how closely it felt to riding normally. Even the little bit of wobble made it feel like a real ride. It didn't take me long to figure out which gear(s) to ride in.
2. Noise was not a problem: I wore earbuds with active noise isolation and listened to podcasts and music. I really didn't hear any background noise from the roller. Because I wore earbuds with active noise isolation, any noise generated by the product was utterly negligible.
3. Varied difficulty by changing gears: I didn't need the worthless tensioner as I simply changed gears on my bike to change the level of difficulty of pedaling. Again, this made it seem even more like a real ride.
4. Price can't be beat: given everything on the "pro" side, the price was so low that it made it very worthwhile to take the risk.

TBD: durability... I have no clue how long this product will continue to perform as it did so well on the first ride.

query: I'm looking for grips that can help alleviate hand numbness during long rides on my hybrid bike. I've tried other grips and gloves, but I still experience discomfort after 30-40 minutes. I've heard that the Ergon GP5 grips have a larger hand rest pad and adjustable positions for added comfort. However, I had some issues with installation because the grips seemed to slip on my handlebar. Can you provide advice on how to install them securely without rotation, and if others have had similar experiences with their grip installation? I want to ensure I get the best comfort while riding.
ori_review:
I have a hybrid/comfort bike for exercising in the evenings and weekends. I already have a pair of large hand grips with extended pad; but, still had hand numbness after 15-20 minutes of riding. I upgraded my gloves to OutdoorMaster Half Finger with Shock-absorbing Gel Pad and that got me up to 30-40 minutes before numbness would start to hit. The Ergon GP5 have a larger hand rest pad to spread the pressure and I like the handles to change your hand position for added comfort without sacrificing control of the bike. I'm still playing with the best handle position for comfort; but, I like them a little higher up than in the near horizontal setting.

The handle bar hole on the Ergon grips seemed to be a touch too big or my handle bar is a touch too small in diameter because the Ergon grips slipped on with not a lot off effort and rotated freely once I put my palms on them. I experimented with double wrapping black electrical tape the length of the grips on the handle bar and using hair spray to lubricate the bar/tape (YouTube trick). The grips went on with some resistance and took some effort once the hair spray started to evaporate after a while to adjust for the most comfortable hand/palm angle. I also had to insert the grips all the way to the end where the handle bar ends were near to the Ergon adjustable hand grip hold attaches with the Allen topped screw. If not, the Ergon handles will come loose/off when riding. Because of this, the supplied decorative end caps were too long to insert; but, no-one will notice. I have no grip rotation when riding and the handles are very secured on the ends. You may not have the same issue with your bike like I did.

I even ordered a 2nd pair for the wife's bike because I like the improvement in comfort so much.

I've used this candle lantern inside the house for at least two weeks now, and I'm pleased with this purchase. I read other reviews about the bottom falling out, but I did not have that problem. You do have to twist the base until it clicks into place, then the base is locked in.

The glass is held in at three friction points, and I did have to tweak the metal pieces that held it into place just a bit. I did this with the glass out of the unit and then slid it back into place. No problems with the glass since then.

It is a candle lantern and if you have kids you should make sure their curiosity doesn't lead them to touch the metal top as it is hot. I have not used this outside and I'm not sure how well it would work, as any major movement of the lamp may cause the wax to spill out into the lower compartment. I would recommend using care when inserting the tea candle so you don't bend the metal pieces that hold it into place. Also, when attaching the lantern cover to the base, do so with gentle firmness so that the tea candle doesn't pop out of its cradle. If it does, pop it back in and replace the cover.

I like this lamp and I will be buying another one as well as UCO's original candle lantern.

query: I'm looking for a tactical belt that offers good value for money, ideally around $25. I want something that is well-built and comfortable, but I have some concerns about the molly system being too loose and the Velcro not matching industry standards. Can I expect this belt to hold up well under a load of 15-20 lbs, and will it work well with other magazine pouches I might want to use in the future? Also, how does it compare to more expensive options?
ori_review:
So let me start by saying this a an AMAZING BELT FOR THE MONEY!!! If you're looking for a CHEAP and for the money an amazing deal. Buy with confidence after you read the pros and cons to see if its right for you.

That said a 25 dollar belt is NOT going to stack well against 150-250 belt systems. I will try to get photos of my Ronin Tactical belt and compare it directly to this belt. It doesn't stack up amazingly. But for shooters or airsofters who want a well built belt but are restricted by income this is a great option.

Pros:

Its a tactical belt for 25 bucks! And it doesn't fall apart as soon as you lock it.

Inner belt webbing is comfortable with a soft grip so it won't rotate on you.

Seems to be built extremely well for the money.

Has a Cobra Locking System.

Double or maybe Triple stitched is most areas.

Love to help out an American Veteran anytime I can.

CONS:
Has 2 major ones in my book.

The molly system is too loose from top, middle, and bottom. The molly system is also too soft and not ridged enough. What does this mean? When you web in single magazine pouches there is quite a bit of play side to side. Which feeds to the second issue.

By having loose molly webbing it will cause a weighted magazine pouch to pull the already too loose webbing forward. I believe this over the long term will cause issues. This is my option

Another gripe from me is the Velcro is not industry norm. In the tactical belt or war belt community the outer belt has male Velcro and the inner belt is female Velcro. I have 2 other battle belts, and wanted to try this belt with a inner belt fed through my belt loops. Because the Velcro isn't industry norm it would be female (soft Velcro side) on female.

Finally I wouldn't want more than 15-20LBS on this belt. But this goes for all warbelts that don't have a locking inner belt.

Final Thoughts:

Mission dictates gear. I can't help new shooters with this enough. With the Cons above how am I giving this 5 stars?!? Because I can live with the cons from a 25 dollar warbelt. I had some extra mag pouches and wanted to make a truck belt that if it got stolen I wouldn't cry about it. I can also let friends borrow this when shooting for fun drills. This belt is amazing for the price.

If you are restricted by funds I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this belt. I would recommend buying name brand magazine pouches. So if you do step up from this belt in the future you don't need to purchase higher quality mag pouches.

I will be uploading photos and a video review shortly.

It has good acceleration, stability and control TH headlight is very bright and works great out in in or area with no street lights. The scooter is quite, I drove right up onto a small heard of 7 deer and was about 10 feet away before they noticed me at all. I am enjoying and The family is as well. I have not tried hauling it around at all yet, But I have seen other local commuters in downtown Houston with the same unit and they also love them. I event saw a petite lady with hers over a shoulder strap on the train, so it seems really doable.

Field Tip for scooters in general:
Just a little something extra to consider.
I did notice that units like these are a lot rougher on my knees in rougher surfaced areas like cobble stones and really old patchwork pavement, these units can be murder on the knees. Our local roads were just repaved 6 months ago so this unit is perfect for here and for me. I also consider that he fast he unit is capable of going the more important this is.

Faster should mean larger wheels also, The faster the unit can go then the larger the wheels should be. The larger the wheel are governs the center of gravity which affects over all stability. Any instabilities are magnified by three conditions. 1) the distance between the axles (length), 2) the diameter of the wheels and 3) speed. Longer scooters with larger wheels are more stable at speed.

Front wheel drive is safer that rear wheel drive .

Direct drive is more simple and reliable than chain or belt drive.

That about sums up what I learned.

query: I'm looking for a high-quality leather lifting belt that will last a long time but is also reasonably priced, ideally under $50. I've done a lot of research and found that a 4" non-tapered belt is recommended. I'm curious if this belt comes with a warranty, as I've seen some similar options offer a lifetime warranty. Also, I want to know if the belt provides good support and comfort during heavy lifts, especially for squats and deadlifts. Can anyone share their experiences with this product regarding its fit and performance?
ori_review:
This review is for the ProFitness leatherlifting belt in small. I am in no way affiliated with this company or vendor, and I was not provided anything in exchange for this review.

Before buying this belt, I did extensive research on lifting belts. I wanted a leather belt that would last for life, but I also didn't want to pay over $50. The Inzer Forever Belts, while really nice, were just a tad out of my price range. Perusing Reddit and fitness forums, folks seemed to suggest a 4" non-tapered leather belt, so that was my goal.

After all my research, it came down to this belt and the Dark Iron Fitness leather lifting belt. From what I can tell from pictures, the two seem nearly identical apart from price (the ProFitness was a few dollars cheaper and had free same-day shipping) and the fact that the Dark Iron Fitness includes a lifetime warranty. I don't see any mention of a warranty on the ProFitness belt, and since I didn't notice the warranty on the Dark Iron Fitness until after purchasing this belt, I hope I don't regret my decision. I'm going to ask the vendor to clarify whether the ProFitness belt includes a warranty.

MATERIAL - The leather is very thick yet pliable. It feels much more expensive than it actually cost and has a nice quality suede backing.

STYLING - The logo is a tad large but is simple enough. I actually kind of like it. The red contrasting stitching looks really great against the black leather and won't show dirt quite like white stitching would (part of why I chose the red).

BUCKLE - I'm glad that I opted for a double buckle. The buckle is very sturdy without being too heavy or bulky. It feels nice on and doesn't pinch, even when I'm carrying a little extra fluff around the midsection. I feel like I could like a ton of weight and the buckle would never fail on me. I do wish there were a small leather flap under the buckle like I've seen with a few other leather lifting belts, which would prevent the inevitable cold shock when the metal buckle touches bare skin in the case of my shirt riding up.

FIT - Measured at navel level, my true waist measures 30.5" without cinching the tape measurer, so I decided on a small. This was the right choice. During lifts, I cinch the belt to the third set of holes from the end, which seems to serve a nice balance between not being able to breathe and having enough abdominal pressure. If I wear the belt over a thicker top or coat, the second set of holes works nicely.

PERFORMANCE - I definitely saw an immediate improvement in my lifts, particularly squats. The belt allowed for exceptional intrabdominal pressure, and it kept my form tight. I instantly added weight to all my lifts. So far, I've used the belt for squats, deadlifts, and overhead press, and my form feels a lot more solid during max sets. I initially experienced some slight pinching during deadlifts, but I played with the position of the belt a bit, and it doesn't seem to be a problem now.

All in all, this is a very solid, well-made leather lifting belt. I expect this to last for a long time and will hopefully update my review as a use this throughout the next few years.

EDIT: I talked with Troy, the lovely gentleman who sells these belts, and it does come with a lifetime warranty. Highly recommend this product based on customer service alone - his responses were prompt and very friendly. Five stars.

query: I've been using Osprey packs for years, and I'm curious about the new Exos 38. How does it compare in comfort and weight to the previous model, especially for summer backpacking trips? Are the improvements in the top lid and side pockets worth it? Also, I’ve had issues with hydration tube routing—does this model have a better setup for that? Lastly, how does the padding in the shoulder straps and hip belt feel during long treks? I'd appreciate any insights on whether this pack is a good choice for 2-3 day weekend trips.
ori_review:
Let me begin by stating I'm been using Osprey packs of various types for a long time and I own and regularly use the previous model of this pack the Exos 46L. Even with that in mind I'm still objective in my assessments and if function is not up to par or quality is lacking somewhere I will point it out.

Here are my observations:
This pack is extremely light. Ok, maybe like the old model its still not up to UL purists standards but I believe one would be hard pressed to match the load capactiy and overall comfort this pack offers. It has a lot more features and comfort bulit-in from the old model and still manages to weigh less.
There are significant improvements with the top lid/pouch. Often times I find I just don't need the top lid/pouch and I remove it to save weight and streamline my pack, this is a nice feature and carry-over from the old model. But, I believe the top lid is now easier to detach and reattach from the old model. This alone is a great feature of these packs. My favorite new feature of the lid design though is that the new model incorporates a sewn in flap with the Osprey logo so that if you do remove the top lid, you still have a functional flap that uses the same fasteners to cover the top of your pack. Way to go Osprey on this one.
The pouches on the hip belt are roomy and no longer mesh. I do not like the fact that the mesh on my old model allows dirt and debris into those pockets, this issue has now been addressed.
The expanding mesh pockets on the sides of the pack have been addressed as well. The mesh is now a finer weave less prone to snagging and ripping and also I feel more easily expandable. Those mesh side pockets on the old model are practically useless with a full pack. One may force a Nalgene bottle in there, but with a full pack and a tight fit there is no way you will get the bottle out while wearing your pack. Also, every time you force a bottle or something in there there is a good chance you will tear the mesh. The new mesh is much improved. Still not an easy task to get a bottle in and out of there but much, much, better.
The new padding incorporated in the the shoulder straps and hip belt is oh so cushy. I can't believe how comfortable the suspension is on this pack. My old 46L is super comfortable too up to about 26-27lbs for me, but this new padding blows away the old model and still somehow manages to be lighter in construction. I can load this pack if I want to the gills, but the straps still won't dig into my shoulders or hips like the old model will start to do under heavy (for the pack) loads. I don't overload my packs for actual treks, but on occasion for training hikes will do so to test me and the pack.
Like the old model, lots of straps and attachment points for various equipment. Weight savers will want to remove these but the little bit of extra weight on an already light and comfortable platform does not bother me and I tend to use these lashing straps.
Now for a minor complaint. The pouches sewn into the shoulder straps are not easy for me to access while wearing the pack and of course they are also small. Think carefully about uses for these pouches as I feel one is pretty limited in what you can put in there. My suggestions would be small travel size bottles of sunscreen or insect repellent and lip balm.
There is no D-ring for routing of the hydration tube on the shoulder strap. The loop sewn into the strap is really tight for this so do yourself a favor and get the magnetic clip that attaches to your drinking tube. Great invention and totally worth it if you regularly use a hydration sleeve with your pack. [[ASIN:B007TJ5X8E Source Tactical Gear Magnetic Tube Clip (Black)]]

Final thought: I bought this pack for the warm months where my Exos 46L is too much pack for what I do. For my summertime treks the new Exos 38 is the answer. I can't believe the comfort of this pack given it's weight. Even fully loaded it's like it's not even there. For me Osprey packs just fit. I realize this is not the case for everyone but it's like my Exos 38 and 46 were custom made for me. It's also hard to beat the "Almighty Guarantee," but I have not had reason to use it yet. If you are in the market for a pack specifically for summertime weekend long 2-3 day backpacking treks then give this pack a hard look. For two days in most cases I can go without the top lid/pouch and three days treks are a breeze with the lid added.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable and lightweight hammock that comes with an integrated mosquito net. I want to ensure it keeps bugs out while I relax outdoors, especially in areas where mosquito-borne viruses are a concern. It would be great if the hammock is easy to set up and can be used without the netting as well. Can you recommend something that fits these needs?
ori_review:
I originally purchased one of these from Woot, but my wife and I kept arguing over who got to use it so I had to buy a second one. For those that tend to be mosquito bite prone, this thing is a godsend. The first time we brought it with us on vacation, we were staying in a small cabin with no AC and I got a bad cold. It was way too hot in the cabin to rest, and the mosquitos were terrible outside. However, I laid a blanket down in the bottom of the hammock (to prevent mosquitos from biting through the bottom), zipped up the netting, and was able to get the extra sleep I needed without a single bit.

The hammock is comfortable, strong, lightweight, and packs up really small in the integrated stuff sack. It's easy to hang, although it doesn't come with any straps or rope (I use a couple of old nylon webbing belts that I can stuff inside the sack, but you can get fancier straps on Amazon). The netting is held up by can elastic cord that runs through two parallel rows of loops, so you end up with more room inside the mosquito net than in other netted hammocks that only use a single string throw one row of loops. The hammock is designed to be used between two trees, where the width of the trunk separates the two elastic lines that support the net, but you can easily use a short stick to separate them if you're hanging it from a poll or hook. The black netting provides plenty of visibility and airflow, and seems to keep the bugs out. The netting is permanently attached, but if you don't want to use it you can turn the hammock upside down so that the netting hangs below it.

Now that EEE, West Nile, zika, chikungunya, and other mosquito-borne viruses are becoming a larger threat, this hammock is a great way to enjoy the great outdoors without worry.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable camping mattress that provides good insulation from the cold ground. Additionally, how responsive is the customer service if I encounter any issues?
ori_review:
I did a lot of tent camping last year and used a roll up exercise mat and decided it was time to upgrade. After lots of online shopping I decided on the Sound Asleep Camping mattress. From the reviews I had read that stated that the mattress stretches the first night, making it feel like it loses air, I decided to air it up at home and leave it for a day to take care of that. I contacted the manufacturer and they sent me a new pump right away. And they stayed in contact to make sure it got to me when it was supposed to! Since the temperature was supposed to get into the low 40s overnight and air mattresses don't usually offer any insulation from the cold ground I inflated the mattress, which takes maybe 3 minutes with the supplied pump, then I put a fitted sheet on it, then a blanket over that for insulation and then my sleeping bag on top of that. Most comfortable I have been camping tent.

A cool feature of the pump is that the inlet and outlet are the same size so it also helps to deflate the mattress when you are ready to go, it sucks the air out of it. No waiting 10 minutes for it to deflate or having to lay on it trying to push the air out of it.

Will it last forever? I mean it inflates and goes on the ground so eventually I'm sure it will leak like any other but it is noticeably heavier than an air mattress I used to have that was designed for indoor use so I would imagine it is quite a bit tougher.

I'm a happy customer.

ori_review:
Over the years, I've owned 3 pair of the original Pro-X, one pair of Pro-X2 and now these Pro-Rugged kneepads.
I'm a Colorado Frontrange based mountain biker, and go between chill afternoon rides with friends to more aggressive back country multi-hour adventures (@iRideDumb, if you're into that type of thing)...
I continue choosing the G-Form kneepads, because I choose to ALWAYS trail ride with kneepads, and the G-Form pads have been comfortable enough and stay in place, so that I barely notice them on my rides.

The original Pro-X seemed to fit small. I choose the XL in order to retain feeling in my legs... They didn't slip, they didn't stretch, and for me they held up really well.

The Pro-X2 seemed to fit larger than the Pro-X. I did one ride with a pair of XL, and while the coverage was better, they slipped down and just didn't fit right for me.

Now to the Pro-Rugged... I ordered size L because of my experience with the Pro-X2, and because these have an adjustable strap at the top.

Sizing-wise, this was the right choice for me! They fit well on my legs, and the strap helps keep 'em in place.
The padding section on the front of the knee is wider and stiffer than the Pro-X... which makes it flare out a little wider than my knee, vs confirming around my knee like the older versions. After 4 rides, they have started loosening up, and I think this will conform more to my leg as they continue to break-in.

Heat-wise, these are slightly warmer in that padding section then the originals. The back of the knee is a mesh fabric, which is lighter than the original, and more breathable... so long hot days, you'll notice 'em more, but only just.

Weight/bulk-wise, these are a little heavier/bulkier than the original... but not super noticeable once you have them on.

All in all, these are a great upgrade from the original Pro-X and Pro-X2. They provide better coverage over the knee, and remain comfortable enough to keep them on the entire time during long warm rides!

query: I'm looking for tips on how to successfully use a refillable hand warmer, specifically regarding the lighting process. I've noticed some negative reviews about difficulty in getting the burner to light properly. How can I ensure that I’m following the correct steps and giving it enough time to work effectively? Any advice on the initial lighting and how to maintain it would be greatly appreciated!
ori_review:
I see a lot of negative reviews for this thing. The problem I think is their lack of patience with a new burner. I purchased this and a spare burner, because they do eventually go out (though it takes a long while) and having a backup for when that happens is nice. My first thought about why so many negative reviews exist for this thing is lack of patience and not heeding the instructions. After pouring the lighter fluid inside the little tank WITHOUT the burner on, replace the burner and the cap and let it sit upright for about two minutes. This lets the fluid vapor finish soaking through the cotton and padding and allow the fumes to lightly saturate the catalyst in the burner. The burner isn't going light right if you don't give it a few minutes EVERY. TIME. YOU FILL IT.

And yet still, on first light (maybe even the second light) with a brand new burner, the burner doesn't play nice. You have to apply that flame for a good 10 or more seconds like the instructions say. (If you're doing it at night or in the dark, the orange glow from the catalyst shows it's lit. If you're lighting during the day time, find a dark corner or cup your hand round the cap and look through the holes, you should see something that resembles an ember despite the daylight) After the burner has gone through roughly an hour of burning (and perhaps even less than that) from then on the catalyst lights very quickly and stays hot for the full 12 hours that it should. You just gotta break the little fella in; I have two now.

query: I'm looking for a compact tire pump that can easily fit in my motorcycle tank bag and work well with tight spaces around the valve stem. I noticed the gauge may not be very accurate, but I want to ensure it can still inflate my motorcycle tires effectively without the hassle of using a larger compressor. Also, how does the locking mechanism work? I want to avoid any confusion when using it during my trips.
ori_review:
You will think you are missing parts, I ordered a 2nd one thinking I was. You're not, just configure the head to how the cardboard sleeve shows. If you're using it on tires you will need to switch the inside part around.
On the lip (locking mechanism on head) UP is Locked, DOWN is Unlocked. So flip the lip DOWN, put the head over your valve stem, flip lip UP once it's on to lock it in place. Yes this is prob opposite of every tire infiltrator you have ever used. This product happens to be reversed. When you are done airing your tire, flip the lip DOWN and wiggle it off the valve stem.
It doesn't feel like it's going to go on at first, just flip the lip Down and wiggle it on, the rubber will stretch around your valve stem I promise.

query: I'm looking for a fitness tracker that accurately monitors sleep and heart rate, especially for my 12-year-old daughter who has started playing sports. ori_review:
Daughter has started playing sports and like many pre-teens doesn't have the best sleep habits. One of the great things about this tracker is the aftermarket bands available, i.e. huge color variety, which are important to her fashion sense, lol. The orange one was on sale, so I got that and she immediately swapped it out for an aftermarket white band (came in a bag of 20 different colors for about 10 bucks!)
Anyways, I was skeptical that the sleep tracking would work, but it does seem to fairly accurately track her total sleep time. We've turned it into a little game where every day we compare who got more sleep. That said, I am skeptical of the sleep details, just as I am skeptical of the sleep details on my fitbit--by that I mean the deep vs. light vs rem sleep...I just have doubts that any of the trackers are really accurate with that, but I think they can get a good ballpark on total sleep time.
The bpm and blood ox seem ok, but seem to read a little slow. She has thin wrists (almost to the last hole on the strap) and likes to wear it a little loose, so maybe that affects it. We go jogging and my fitbit instantly has my bpm but hers needs a few seconds to read. (I think she may have an app setting that only checks every 1 minute)
The app has a ton, ton of tweaks and settings the user can play with to change how it works, a lot of them oriented towards battery life versus data capture. She had no problem figuring out the settings, getting texts to show on the watch, and changing the face graphics to her liking.
I am still getting life out of my 3 or 4 year old fitbit inspire HR, but if/when it dies I'll go with this or whatever its latest version is at the time. Fitbit has gotten too greedy moving premium features to subscription, I really like this band as you buy once, and nothing is paywalled.

query: I'm looking for a versatile tarp that can handle light rain and strong winds, especially for car camping and backyard use. How easy is it to set up by myself, and are there any tips to ensure it stays secure and doesn't damage the fabric while packing it away? ori_review:
Super easy to set up once you have done it a few times. Some reviews here have said that it's difficult without two people but if you follow the instructions which say to stake down the back two corners and then the front two corners you're solid. Do not attempt to put back pole up inside of the tent - it will tear through the tent fabric -- Instructions/pictures are not clear about having the back pole on the exterior of the back mesh wall. Another thing to ensure that it taught enough ...is ensuring the measurement and placement of front corners.

Super easy to set up. I have only used it in my backyard a few times but it held up perfectly through a few light rain showers and some solid wind gusts. It worked well in keeping sun out -- living in South Carolina we get some hot days even in February -- it worked will in that regard especially with the mesh bottom portions of the side walls that also have the vents on both sides, and the entire side triangular back wall is mesh allowing a maximized flow of air.

There is one tiny con, but it's more of a user error. It's important to fold it back small and tight and ensure you don't snag the bag zipper on the tent fabric because it will catch on the fabric if not super delicate when packing back up -- so don't speed through packing up. I will say a good strategy to avoid this is packing the tent/tarp first then placing the stake/guy line/pole bags on top of the tent so when you zip if it catches on any fabric it will be the fabric of the light weight bag enclosed to hold the poles.

I would highly recommend for any type of light daily use in parks, sporting events, tailgating (although you must have enough space since it is rather large), car camping, or even in the backyard for the kids to have a little shade while running around the neighborhood during a sunny day.

The powder did it's job. other people have mentioned similar products you can find at RV supply stores I'm not sure if there is a cheaper more generic bulk product that might be less expensive if you use this regularly, but for my trip this package was more than enough I could have probably used half given the wag bags already started with some in them. query: I'm looking for a high-quality survival knife with a serrated edge, and I've heard great things about the Gerber Prodigy Tanto. Additionally, any insights on whether the handle material feels sturdy would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Bought from Amazon, shipped/sold by Amazon.

Just recently i got bit by the blade bug (it was quite painful), and I've been building a small collection of what i would like to call my "survival/home defense kit".

Gerber has been around for some time now and even though they have factories in China (still awesome Gerber knives made in China), Their high-end made knives are manufactured in Oregon. They've been making knives for the US Army since the 1960's..

I have a few Gerber pocket knives all in which are made in China, but that doesn't necessarily make them bad, they are actually all damn good with very sharp blades..

This one, called the Prodigy is made superbly, it feels wicked in the hand, the steel and just overall build quality and feel is pretty damn great! The tanto point with serrated edge is really nice and really makes it look sexy!
The blade is sharp, but not ultra sharp. it definitely needs to get professionally re-edged!
The edge of the blade out of the box was perfect, not chipped or rounded, straight lines all the way through!

It's full tang all the way down to the butt of the handle and even that looks like it would mess somebody's day up real bad.

The grip/handle is good but not great! I have the Strong Arm Gerber knife and the grip on that beast beats this one leaps and bounds!
The Tac-Hide material feels a bit thin, not crappy thin, just thin. It's strong to a point, just don't abuse it.
The butt end of this knife where the grip material ends seems like its peeling, it's just a hair bit, but i wont mess with it and it should stay on.
The plastic mold is solid, it does look like a 2 piece mold though.

The sheath is super ultra tight with knife inserted, hopefully it weakens overtime. Great to know it wont fall out by accident or force!
Sheath is bi-directional, so you can insert it point in with blade left or right.

It's really just so affordable, not cheap!

Update**, i bought another one! So i now have 2 Prodigy Tanto's!

Picture i uploaded is of the Gerber Prodigy Tanto, Gerber Strong Arm Spear Point, and Bear Grylls Compact Fixed Blade.

ori_review:
I have an FT7 and I bought this FT4 for my wife. As far as I can tell the FT7 only adds the ability to connect to a computer if you buy an additional part. So I do not really see it worth the extra money.

Both the FT7 and FT4 connect with the chest heart rate monitor right out of the box no setup required and they very accuratly. Below is my review for the FT7 which holds true for the FT4

I am a personal trainer and I always had my clients estimate their calorie burn during workouts using a one of the many free calculators on the web. I just got one of these for myself and I am very impressed. I will be recommending it to all of my clients who want to accurately track their calorie burn during workouts.
I use it to keep myself honest during my workouts and to help push myself.
Pros
- easy to use and setup, I did not need to read the manual to figure it out
- I was concerned that pairing it with the chest monitor would be a pain, but it came paired in the box.
- it is accurate, and a heart rate monitor is the only way to accurately measure calorie burn
Cons
- It has some sort of light sensor so it turns on the light when you hit any button in a dark space. While that is nice I would like to be able to turn it off to save battery. There is a separate light button.
Other comments
-I have only used it a week so I cannot comment on the battery life, but the battery is easy to replace and uses a standard battery.
- The screen is a little low rez and could use some more contrast. However its very readable and a better screen would have add more cost.

Overall I would recommend this device for anyone looking to track their workouts more accurately.

Update
Some reviews and other information on the web comment on the inaccuracy of heart rate monitors for workouts. Let's say you did a one hour workout and burned 600 calories according to the watch. You have to subtract the number of calories you would have burned in a normal hour from the 600 to get an accurate net calorie burn.
So if you typically burn 100 calories an hour 600-100 = 500 extra calories from working out.

query: I'm looking for a jump rope that is lightweight and designed for speed, ideally one that allows for quick spinning and is suitable for advanced techniques like double-unders. I’ve heard some ropes can be hard to feel when swinging, which affects timing and rhythm. Is there a way to adjust the rope length easily, and how does the customer service of the company handle feedback on their products? Additionally, is it true that this type of rope isn’t recommended for beginners and requires some practice to get used to?
ori_review:
First off, this jump rope is great and terraFIT has the best customer service evar! They actually take customer feedback into account when designing/re-designing products!

Anyway, everything about this thing is small/svelte. The handles are small in diamter and very light, and the rope is a thin cable that is coated in plastic. The handles are an outer black plastic piece, with an inner white plastic piece that rotates and is connected to the rope. There is an adjustment in the handle to change how much movement/"play" there is between the two parts of the handle, and you want to double check that it is set loose enough for the inner white plastic piece to rotate freely.

The rope simply slides through eyelets at the ends of the handles and has two small metal stops that let you adjust the length of the rope, which you WILL need to do (it comes pretty long). They advise that once you have the rope length adjusted that you cut it to suit, so you don't have a bunch of extra rope swinging around.

The carrying case is a really nice touch.

All in all this is a fantastic jump rope that can achieve some crazy speeds because of how thing / light it is, VERY easy to spin it quick enough for double-unders. On the other hand the rope is so light that you pretty much cannot feel it swinging around you. IT IS VERY DIFFERENT THAN A ROPE BASED JUMP ROPE that you may have used in elementary school. A normal thick rope is easy to feel swinging around your body so you can pretty much feel when you should jump. WIth this TerraFit rope you MUST develop a rythym because you cannot tell where the rope is at very well. This is a skill that will take some time to develop if you aren't used to jumping rope a lot.
I read the reviews that said "not for beginners" and didn't understand what they meant, but it's the heft/weight of the rope that makes all the difference in the technique that you have to use. Once you get used to it though it's great!

End of the day this rope is worth buying for 3 reason 1) you can spin it super fast 2) it comes with a spare rope 3) terrafit is an awesome company.

query: I'm looking for a high-quality poncho liner that is made in the USA, but I'm concerned about the price. I want to know if the quality justifies the cost, especially compared to cheaper options that I've used before. How do the materials, stitching, and durability compare, and would it be worth it for field use despite being overpriced? Also, are there alternatives to buying new that still meet high standards?
ori_review:
This is a genuine, US made poncho liner, and the quality is top notch. However I do feel that it is way overpriced. It should cost no more than $50-$60. That said, I’ll note the differences between this genuine liner (henceforth referred to as “US” liner) and my USGI industries (made in China) liner (henceforth referred to as “China” liner) so that you can decide if it is worth purchasing for the insane price.
1. The stitching - the stitches on the US liner are closer together (I.e. there are more stitches per inch of fabric) and hence it is stronger and will stand more abuse than the China liner.

2.the trim around the liner perimeter - on the China liner, there is a gap where the trim overlaps itself, large enough to fit a finger or pen into it. This can potentially get snagged on something and result in a tear. On the US liner, wherever the trim overlaps itself the overlap is sewn shut, so there is no chance of it snagging. Also, on the US liner, the stitching that connects the trim to the main blanket is stitched higher up from the edge of the trim than on the China liner. This will prevent the fabric of the trim from coming loose easily. The trim stitching on the China liner is very close to the edge of the trim material.

3. The ropes/tie-outs - on US liner, the tie-outs are made of genuine, gutted milspec paracord. The China liner is made of some kind of synthetic rope material that is obviously not as strong and robust as the paracord and looks like it would easily fray/wear out from heavy use. The bartack stitching used to attach the tie outs to the liner is also more robust and better done on the US liner.

4. The Filling - the US liner has noticeably more filling than the China liner

These are the main differences that I’ve noticed. I wanted a liner that I could trust in the field, so I bit the bullet and bought this, but at home I sleep with my China liner. I’ve had the China liner for less than a year and some of the stitching is already beginning to come out. And that is simply from using it as a blanket on my bed. For home use, the China liner is definitely worth it due to its much lower price tag. If you want a genuine US quality liner for harder use, then you have to decide for yourself if it us worth paying double what the liner is worth. Another option is to buy a used one in good condition. You can get them around $40-$50 if you are Lucky. I hope this review was helpful.
In summary, it is top quality, but extremely overpriced

query: I'm looking for a portable and versatile travel spinning setup that can complement my travel casting setup. I want something that is easy to set up and break down, with good line markers. I've been looking for a versatile travel spinning setup to compliment my travel casting setup and this has been on my radar for some time. I took the leap and bought it based on reviews and gave it a true test. I went to a couple of my honey holes and caught some decent sized bass. My initial thought is that this setup and breakdown is a breeze on this rod and the line markers do help line things up. The finish reminds me of my 13 Fishing Omen rod and I love it! Make sure to spool your line without line twist because the first eyelet isn't that standard huge guide we're used to and may possibly limit cast distance. While fishing I was able to feel everything from rocks, ledges, grass and stumps. I even felt blue gil nipping at my senko! It's almost comparable to my high end rigs! When I got a fish on (you can feel the bite it's wonderful) I was able to muscle the bass out of vegetation and then I tested the back bone out for boat flipping and durability. It passed those tests with flying colors.

In the end, I highly recommend this rod and will be using it when going on trips where I can't bring my main setups or when I go scout ponds for bass.
